details:
WHAT IT DOES
Marswalk is an interactive tool for planning a safe astronaut walk on Mars. It layers four NASA datasets on a single map of Jezero Crater and checks a planned route against hazards in real time. Users can draw, drag and edit a route, and the app instantly reports the distance, estimated walking time and clearance from each hazard as CLEAR, CAUTION or CONFLICT. It also compares the out-and-back time against an EVA time budget and flags routes that go over it.

HOW IT WORKS
The map combines MRO CTX imagery for terrain detail, MGS MOLA elevation hillshade, Mars Odyssey THEMIS thermal infrared and the Viking colour mosaic, all from NASA/JPL Mars Trek. Each layer can be toggled and blended with its own opacity slider. Science targets and hazard zones (soft dunes, a steep scarp slope and boulder terrain) are drawn at true scale. Distances and clearances are calculated on a Mars-radius sphere (3,396,190 m) rather than Earth's. Perseverance and Jezero photos from the NASA Image and Video Library add ground-level context. Routes can be exported as GeoJSON.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Mission planners and crews usually have to switch between separate tools to see terrain, science targets and danger zones. Marswalk puts them in one view and gives immediate feedback while a route is being edited, so a path that clips a hazard is obvious before anyone commits to it. The aim is to make surface-excursion planning faster, clearer and safer, and to make real NASA data easy for non-specialists to explore.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES
Python and Flask for the backend and API, JavaScript with Leaflet for the interactive map, HTML and CSS for the interface, the Requests library for NASA data, and pytest for automated tests. Data comes from NASA/JPL Mars Trek and the NASA Image and Video Library.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES
Rather than only displaying data, Marswalk turns it into a planning tool, with live safety feedback as the route changes. The mission is defined once on the backend and the frontend renders exactly what the API returns, so the map and the sidebar can never disagree. Imagery is cached, and if NASA is unreachable the app says so instead of showing fabricated content.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Safety was the main design driver, followed by honesty about the data. Target, hazard and route positions are approximate planning locations, not surveyed data, and the walking speed (2 km/h) and 240-minute EVA budget are labelled as assumptions. The pressure and radiation figures in the header are published reference values and are marked as not live. Radiation exposure along a route is not yet modelled.

NEXT STEPS
Radiation zones with dwell-time limits, slope-aware auto-routing from elevation data, a HiRISE close-up layer, and real target and hazard coordinates from CRISM and HiRISE products.
